title: How to Build Strong Relationships with Students if You're Starting the Year Online -online-principles-and-practices
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. addresses teachers panicked about building relationships with students they've never met in person, grounding the piece in three principles: teachers already know practices that work in-person, relationships are a reward of teaching rather than its point, and relationships aren't automatically hampered by distance the way some fear. He defines what he's actually after in a teacher-student relationship — interpersonal circumstances that promote motivation, engagement, and productivity — before offering three practices: rapid memorization of student names and interests via index cards, a remote-adapted version of his "moments of genuine connection" (MGC) tracking system, and regular positive phone calls to parents. Stuart gives concrete remote-teaching examples for each practice, such as using a Zoom waiting room to deliver brief individual MGCs, before closing with additional tips drawn from Hattie, Fisher, and Frey's Distance Learning Playbook.
points: Stuart reframes the challenge by insisting teachers already possess relationship-building expertise from in-person teaching that can be "remote-ified" rather than reinvented from scratch.
His MGC system is defined by eight explicit criteria (brief, scheduled, balanced, tracked, inclusive, aimed at specific feelings, attempted rather than guaranteed, and authentic).
A concrete remote-teaching example — using Zoom's Waiting Room to deliver 30-second individual MGCs as students are admitted — shows how an in-person routine transfers to a synchronous online format.
Positive parent phone calls (3-5 per weekday) are framed as a "long-term sanity aid" that builds teacher credibility community-wide with minimal daily time investment.
quotes: First, you know a lot about building relationships with students at the start of the school year. Grab a notebook and write down a few go-to practices you would use if you were going to be starting the school year normally this year.

The work we're used to doing will be different remotely — and in some ways harder — but it won't be impossible. And the sanest place to start, in my opinion, is by thinking about how we might remote-ify what we know works in-person.
Knowledge has a way of begetting relationship. If you and I meet and I learn your name, that's a start — we've gone from stranger to shallow acquaintance.

When Stacey from Wisconsin held her class Zoom sessions in Spring 2020, she used the Waiting Room feature to slowly bring students into the main class session. As she brought students in, she'd attempt an MGC with each one — 30 seconds apiece.
What you're after are positive interactions with parents — sort of like MGCs, except what you want to communicate to the parent is that you value, know, and appreciate their child.
Too often we teachers are blinded to the reality that our fearfully, wonderfully wrought students are not only individuals — they are also human beings influenced by their social contexts.
